#MJ
CA: 0xbd824d3f83c31ab38132bfc76654897c73157777
https://t.co/cJyKQTIYSC

Jensen Huang gets the Michael Jackson treatment, and BSC turns the joke into a token.

That is the hook behind MJ: an AI-generated concert parody, a recognizable tech figure and a name that compresses the whole visual into two letters. “Michael Jensen” gives traders something they can repeat without explaining a product or a complicated mechanism.

The video was circulating before the token chatter. @Bqlsj2023 shared it while discussing AI-generated parody videos, and @shrmodelx posted another version with the caption “Ok it makes sense lmao.” Replies picked up the concert joke, while other users described the character as “Michael Jensen” and “the king of compute.” The meme already had an audience outside token promotion. Source video.

Then came a concrete attention catalyst: Elon Musk replied to the video, “This is why RAM is so expensive” with laughing emojis. That response ties the absurd performance back to the computing resources used to generate it, giving the clip another joke people can share. His interaction concerns the video; it does not announce or endorse MJ. Musk’s reply.

The combination works because the references reinforce each other. Jensen supplies the AI and GPU association. Michael Jackson supplies the stage persona. AI-generated entertainment brings them together. Even someone who has never opened a trading terminal can understand the visual, which gives the underlying meme a broader potential audience than a joke built entirely around a token chart.

BSC traders are adding their own angle: a Chinese crypto account’s video reached Musk, and a locally launched meme is trying to capture that attention. Posts carrying this exact contract repeatedly emphasize that connection. It gives the token a community-specific reason to circulate, although much of the contract-level discussion still consists of scanner alerts, calls and profit screenshots.

MJ launched through Flap and has graduated to PancakeSwap. Its main pool is quoted against NVDAB, adding another NVIDIA reference to the presentation. That pairing is a market detail, not evidence of an NVIDIA relationship.

As of now, MJ sits around a $347K market cap, with roughly $741K in 24-hour volume and 1,090 holders. The recorded volume is concentrated within the past hour. Buy and sell volume are also close—approximately $376K against $366K—so the burst reflects heavy trading in both directions.

The next stage depends on whether “Michael Jensen” becomes a recurring character. Fresh edits, captions and independent reposts would give people reasons to return to the joke after Musk’s reply stops being new. Recycled screenshots of that interaction offer much less room for the story to develop.

There is also competition for the attention: token posts are already circulating both BSC and Solana addresses. A viral video can travel widely while the speculative demand fragments across several coins.

MJ has a clear visual identity and a traceable catalyst. Its staying power rests on whether people keep making and sharing the character—and whether this particular token becomes the place that community gathers.

In a jury trial, the duty of the defence lawyer is to establish reasonable doubt.

In the last six years, many of us have been researching and/or sharing the information that has been uncovered about:

the origin of the virus
the dodgy creation of the vaccine
the lies about the vaccine’s safety and effectiveness
the excess deaths that have occurred after the rollout among the vaccinated
the fact that the unvaccinated population did not die of COVID
and more

QU 04

QU 08
Many economic refugees leave the third world and the developing world looking for a better life. Australia was seen as the Lucky Country, where the great Australian dream was reachable. Now, for many, it is not. So if you had a hankering to leave, list the countries you could flee to that would not only accept you, but would also offer you a chance to reach the dreams you cannot achieve here in the ‘Lucky Country’.

QU 09

QU 10

QU 11
Many cultures are measured by their history and achievements. China, for example, has completely changed its cultural identity, from Little Red Book-carrying backwater communists to the tech leaders of the modern world. America has gone from the bastion of freedom and honour to a never-ending reality-show train wreck. Australia has also changed its identity (as quoted by Alex Antic). QU 12
The Romans changed the world, then collapsed into the Italians. The Napoleonic French changed the world; now the streets of Paris appear to always be on fire. The Commonwealth once appeared to rule the world; now the English are jailing their own citizens for Facebook posts.

Arguably, the base common denominator in the collapse of these superpowers was politics and corruption.

On the other hand, Argentina has travelled from a vicious dictatorship, to a corrupt economic basket case, to a thriving community that is doing well. El Salvador, too, went from one of the most corrupt and dangerous countries on the planet to one of the safest, and a tourist mecca.

text:
🔎The Focus This Week: Earnings Season

Third-quarter earnings season is creeping in, and the bar is way up there.

Last quarter, a whopping 86% beat analysts' profit estimates, with success rates ranging from 68% among utilities to a near-clean sweep of 97% in healthcare.

And talk about improvements: overall profits leaped 52% from a year earlier, their fastest pace in five years.

Every sector except healthcare posted earnings growth, and even stripping out huge one-time gains at Alphabet and Amazon, profits still climbed more than 30%. And those numbers will be tough to outrun.

▶ Analysts lately have been raising their forecasts rather than lowering them. They pushed estimates up by more than 1% between July and September.

That’s a bit weird: over the past decade, they've typically trimmed them by 2.5% over the same stretch. Now, they’re expecting profits to lurch ahead 29% from a year ago, led by energy and tech.

If they’re right, this’ll be the third straight quarter of growth above 25%.

▶ The scary part is that stocks are priced for loads of good news already.

S&P 500 earnings have popped above their long-term trend and pulled well away from the pace of economic growth, making strong growth harder to sustain.

Stocks aren’t cheap: the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio – which gauges whether stocks are overvalued or undervalued using ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings – is lingering near an all-time high.

At the same time, a global bond selloff has sent US Treasury yields to elevations not seen in decades, making safer bonds a more enticing alternative.

▶ A reassuring start would be a welcome treat.

One of the first big names to open its books is Delta Air Lines, and its results could offer an early read on whether consumers are still willing to splash out on travel despite the squeeze from high prices.

But the bigger test is lurking later in the month, when tech behemoths like Alphabet and Microsoft will reveal whether their enormous AI spending is translating into equally impressive growth.

⚠️ Right now, folks are on edge. Inflation is high, and the Federal Reserve is already hinting at the terrifying prospect of further interest rate hikes that could weigh on the economy.

That only raises the stakes for earnings: US stocks need strong profits across the board to justify their lofty prices, and investors won’t take kindly to any nasty surprises.

text:
Spectrum Business Shows Strong AI and Wireless Growth Potential

Industry Analyst and Strategic Advisor Jeff Kagan provides comment and analysis

As an Industry Analyst, Strategic Advisor and Columnist, I see Spectrum Business is turning up the volume on growth going forward with technology like artificial intelligence, wireless, data networks, entertainment and more.

Traditionally, the cable television industry used to operate with relatively little competitive pressure. Each competitor had a different geographic sector of the United States and their offerings were limited.

However, over the past 25 years, new technologies have created significant competition, new growth opportunities and new challenges. At the same time many new services which they offer compete nationally, not regionally.

Companies such as Spectrum are now focused on adapting their businesses and maintaining their positions as industry leaders while moving into these new areas.

Today, Spectrum Business is focusing on growth opportunities involving wireless, high-speed data, streaming and increasingly AI as this sector continues to grow and evolve.

Charter Communications, the parent company of Spectrum and Spectrum Business. It recently completed its acquisition of Cox cable television assets, making Spectrum larger and expanding its geographic reach to more customers.

The company is focused on growth in wireless, AI, streaming, high-speed Internet and other technology sectors.

Spectrum Business is becoming an increasingly important competitor in the business services marketplace. The growth potential in this sector continues to expand as businesses of all sizes adopt new technologies like AI and need help and assistance on a variety of levels.

The industry continues to change rapidly. While we do not yet know exactly what the industry will look like in the future, who will enter or who the leaders will be, it is good news that companies like Spectrum seem to understand the risks and growth opportunities in front of them and are acting on them.

Going forward, I will keep my eyes on and continue to comment on this fast-changing industry as competitive positioning, growth and leadership continue to evolve.

How should a Christian view relics?
Answer
A splinter from Jesus’ cross has been found in Turkey. Jesus’ baby blanket has surfaced in Germany. The index finger of John the Baptist is now on display in a reliquary in a Missouri museum. Relics—carefully preserved religious artifacts meant to be venerated—have long played a role in many religions, including Christianity. By the Middle Ages, there were hundreds of supposed burial places for the twelve apostles. It has been said that one could build a large boat from all the pieces of wood purported to be from Jesus’ cross. The most famous Christian relic, the Shroud of Turin, attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors each year. Should Christians be interested in relics?

Undeniably, it would be extremely interesting if an actual piece of Jesus’ cross or a thorn from the crown of thorns could be discovered and verified. The problem is that there is absolutely no way to know if a piece of Judean wood dates to the 1st century A.D. Someone could claim it came from Jesus’ cross, but how could that claim be substantiated? The wood could just as easily have come from a Judean fence post. In the early centuries of the Roman Catholic Church, relics became a massive profiteering scam. Seemingly every church throughout Europe had some sort of relic to attract visitors. If a church in a nearby town “discovered” a more important relic, a game of one-upmanship ensued, with the relics being “discovered” becoming more and more impressive. All that to say, it is highly unlikely that any of the Christian relics discovered in the past 2,000 years have any true connection to Jesus or the apostles.

One of the dangers inherent in the veneration of relics is the temptation to commit idolatry. This is exactly what happened in ancient Israel. God had told Moses to make a bronze serpent in order to save the Hebrews from a plague of poisonous snakes (Numbers 21:8–9). That bronze serpent was kept by the Israelites as a reminder of God’s goodness and salvation; however, by the time of King Hezekiah, the “relic” had become an object of worship. Hezekiah’s reforms included breaking “into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had been burning incense to it. (It was called Nehushtan)” (2 Kings 18:4). Physical aids to faith, if not commanded by God, are unnecessary and inevitably lead to superstition and idolatry.

There is absolutely no power in Christian relics. Even if the entire cross of Jesus were discovered intact, it would have no spiritual value. Relics do not, in any manner whatsoever, enable us to get closer to God. The humerus of a saint can do nothing for your spirit. Relics should not be prayed to, worshiped, or in any way be used as a means to better connect with God. Using relics in such a talismanic way is blatant idolatry (Exodus 20:3; Isaiah 42:8). An elaborate church filled with relics is no more valid a place for worship than a simple tent in a jungle. We worship the Lord in spirit and truth (John 4:24), not by idols, icons, or relics, whether genuine or fake.

The pope's apology in Canada was historic, but for some Indigenous people, not enough
Updated July 25, 2022 7:10 PM ET 
By 
Scott Neuman
Years after a Canadian-government-funded commission issued findings detailing a history of physical and sexual abuse of Indigenous children in the country's Catholic-run residential schools, Pope Francis on Monday issued an apology on Canadian soil.

"I am sorry," the pope said, speaking in Maskwacis, Alberta, at the lands of four Cree nations.

"I humbly beg forgiveness for the evil committed by so many Christians against the Indigenous peoples," Francis said near the site of the former Ermineskin Indian Residential School, where ground-penetrating radar has been used to try to locate unmarked graves of students who died while attending the school.

The residential schools forcibly separated Indigenous children from their parents as part of an effort to convert them to Christianity and assimilate them into the wider Canadian culture. In total, 150,000 children from Canada's First Nations tribes were placed in 139 schools run under government contract — most by the Catholic Church — over a 150-year period.

A 2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission report prompted by the harrowing tales of survivors concluded that "[children] were abused, physically and sexually, and they died in the schools in numbers that would not have been tolerated in any school system anywhere in the country."

The schools were designed "not to educate" the Indigenous children, "but primarily to break their link to their culture and identity," the report said. It concluded that the establishment and operation of the schools "can best be described as 'cultural genocide.'"

Officially, 4,120 children died while in the care of the schools, mostly from diseases such as tuberculosis that ran rampant, according to government statistics. But estimates range considerably higher. The commission, in its report, acknowledged that the true number "is not likely ever to be known in full."

Last year, the unmarked graves of 215 children were found on land once occupied by the Kamloops Indian Residential School. At one time, it was the largest residential school in Canada with 500 students enrolled in the 1950s.

Earlier this year, Francis expressed "shame and sorrow" for the Catholic Church's role in abuses and for "the lack of respect" shown to Indigenous cultures and their values.

"It's a step in the right direction," says Congress of Aboriginal Peoples National Chief Elmer St. Pierre of the pope's apology on Monday. But "it could have been better," he says.

"When you sing the song [it should be] coming from your heart," says St. Pierre, who was present in Maskwacis when Francis spoke. Francis' statement was "read off a script," he says.

Canada has paid billions of dollars to Indigenous communities as part of a settlement with some 90,000 survivors of the residential schools. Canada's Catholic Church says its dioceses and religious orders have already paid $50 million to the tribes and expects another $30 million in coming years.

Carol McBride, president of the Native Women's Association of Canada, said she hoped the pope's apology would start a dialogue between the church and First Nations that would lead to the release of school records and the return of tribal artifacts that she says reside at the Vatican. The Holy See insists the headdresses, carved walrus tusks and other items were gifts to Pius XI, who was pope from 1922 until his death in 1939.

Pete Hegseth turned down a West Point offer to play basketball at Princeton. He rode the bench for four years. 42 games, almost all garbage time. He ended up running the Pentagon anyway.

The best story is his senior day. March 8, 2003, against Columbia. Four years of practice reps and spot minutes, and John Thompson III finally calls his number with Princeton stuck in a five minute scoring drought. Hegseth checks in and drains two threes, then assists on the game winner. Princeton wins 44-40 in front of 5,205 at Jadwin.

His quote after the game aged well. "I wasn't going to hesitate to take the shot. I feel that's my strength."

People read "played 1 minute in March Madness" as a diss. Run the funnel instead. Around 540,000 kids play high school basketball every year, roughly 1% of them ever make a Division I roster, only 68 teams reach the tournament, and most guys at the end of those benches never check in at all. One minute of floor time against 2-seed North Carolina puts you in a club of a few thousand people alive.

The order of operations is the part worth sitting with. He skipped West Point for basketball, joined ROTC a few months before 9/11, deployed to Guantanamo, Iraq and Afghanistan, and in 2025 took over the Pentagon. He turned down the academy and ended up in charge of everyone who went.

And judging by the clip, the stroke never left.

SIGNS YOU NEED TO LEAVE YOUR JOB

1. YOUR PAY IS CONSISTENTLY DELAYED
Your salary is always delayed, paid the following month, or you go several months without being paid.

2. YOU ARE EXPECTED TO BE AVAILABLE ALL THE TIME
If weekends, holidays and personal time are treated as company property, you do not have a job with healthy boundaries. You work from Monday to Sunday with no assigned off day. Also, any job where you can't go on official leave is a terrible job.

3. Your organization doesn’t observe public holidays. Even when you work on those days, there are no bonuses or extra compensation.

4. There are no HMO packages for staff.

5. The starting salary for graduates is less than 200,000.

6. There are no clearly defined working hours. On busy days, you’re expected to stay late and work beyond your scheduled hours. In some places, you can’t leave until your boss has gone home. Yet, no one pays you for overtime.

7. THE BEST PEOPLE KEEP LEAVING
Pay attention to who is resigning and why. High employee turnover, especially among competent people, is rarely random.

8. THE COMPANY DOES NOT INVEST IN ITS PEOPLE
No meaningful training, no development, no proper tools and no effort to improve employees can eventually leave you less valuable in the labour market.

9. GOOD PERFORMANCE IS NOT REWARDED
Hardworking employees should be recognised and rewarded for their effort.
Treating them the same as employees who barely do their jobs is discouraging.

10. YOU ARE CONSTANTLY CLEANING UP MANAGEMENT'S MISTAKES
If poor planning and bad decisions by management keep becoming your problem to solve, and you are constantly taking the fall for them, that is a red flag. You should not be taking the blame because someone above you failed to do their job properly.

11. There is no job security. Any job where you can be dismissed outright without a query, a disciplinary hearing, or going through the proper dismissal process is a red flag. They can simply wake up one morning and ask you to go home.

12. Any job where people or customers who know where you work call you and the first thing they ask is, "Are you still working there?"

13. This may be unpopular, but any job where customers regularly tip you is usually not a good job. Most people tip out of pity because they know you're poorly paid, although it can also be a reward for excellent customer service.

14. YOUR RESPONSIBILITIES KEEP INCREASING WITHOUT YOUR COMPENSATION CHANGING
More work and more pressure without a corresponding increase in pay, position or opportunity is not career growth. You are simply being given more work for the same reward.

15. THERE IS NO CLEAR PATH FOR GROWTH
If you have been doing the same thing for years with no meaningful increase in responsibility, compensation, skills or opportunities, you may be stagnating. A job with no clearly defined organizational structure, where you can work for years without any growth or promotion. The only way to move up is if your line manager resigns. A good organization should have clearly defined career progression with different grades or levels for each position. That way, even before you earn a promotion, your salary continues to improve with experience.

16. Any job where staff members don't have official email addresses for communication and escalation.

17. Any job where you're victimized by your superior and have no avenue to seek redress. You're constantly talked down to and treated poorly, yet you're forced to endure it.

18. YOU ARE STAYING ONLY BECAUSE YOU ARE AFRAID TO LEAVE
If the only thing keeping you there is fear of unemployment, start preparing your exit instead of pretending the job is good.

19. Your health and personal life are constantly paying the price.

20. YOU HAVE OUTGROWN THE ORGANIZATION
Sometimes the problem is not that the company is terrible. You have simply reached a point where the organization can no longer offer the growth, challenge, income or opportunities you need.

text:
Most people can see the cost of saying yes.

They see how much money, time, and effort this takes, along with the risk, because it’s right there in front of them, in numbers they can count.

The cost of saying no is invisible.

And invisible costs are the ones that compound.

There’s this story from my book Quiet Persuasion that illustrates this.

Friend of mine was a salesman. He spent 5 years at the same company. The pay was decent, he was comfortable, but didn’t have much opportunity for growth, in responsibilities nor income.

So he started looking around and went through an interview with a smaller company. The interview went well. The job was promising.

But he wasn’t convinced.

Because it meant switching industries, starting over, taking a risk. And he was very comfortable where he was…

So voiced his doubts to the CEO on his way out, right after the interview. The CEO listened carefully, then said something he’d never forget.

“You’re 33 right now. You’re married, no kids. If you want to become a father, chances are it’s happening in the next year or two. So if you switch now, you’ve still got a year, maybe two, to build the right foundations before that happens.”

Brief pause. A friendly stare.

“But if you don’t, you probably won’t make the move once your kid arrives. I’ve seen it happen. Taking care of a baby is work. And men tend to slow down when they become first-time fathers. 

Then around 45 when the kids are more independent they wake up and realize it’s too late. They don’t have the same hunger, the same energy, and they’re competing with 30-year-olds who are just as qualified. Then they become washed up, bitter, praying they don’t lose their job before retirement.”

Then he said, “If you want to make a career move, well, the time is now.”

My friend took the job that week.

The CEO didn’t pressure him, he didn’t negotiate salary nor benefits.

He just made inaction expensive.

He took every hidden cost of staying put, the slow erosion of ambition, the window that closes when children arrive, the 45-year-old version of himself my friend had never considered, and laid them out in a sequence my friend had already seen in some people around him.

The 45+ years-old, washed-up salesmen exist. He’s worked with some of them. He knew them by name.

He just never considered he could end up as one of them.

The CEO’s entire argument was against standing still, not for his company.

And once you can show what standing still really costs over time, acting becomes the obvious move.

Most people selling something focus on making the yes more attractive. They look for better features, offer more bonuses, or make a bigger promise.

But sometimes, the stronger lever is on the other side.

What happens if they don’t act? What erodes? What compounds while they wait?

When you answer this honestly, in a way that speaks to your prospect, when you show him vividly what staying the same costs a year from now, 5 years from now, 10 years from now…

You don’t need to convince them anymore.

The timing does it for you.

text:
ICYMI O/N & WEEKEND

IRAN:

Reuters and Bloomberg sources have both denied reports that suggested the East West pipeline was not running due to an attack over the weekend. (RTRS/BBG)

A US official told Semafor that there is a real possibility that Iran may want to inflict some pain on US President Trump before the midterms, and that Iran may do something in the next couple of weeks. (Semafor)

US VP Vance chaired secret Camp David talks on Iran and Yemen on Friday as Trump weighed renewed major combat operations, US officials told Axios. (Axios)   

Iran is preparing for a potentially larger US bombing campaign but retains the ability to respond, a Tehran official told Bloomberg. The official also said Iran’s economic situation is extremely painful but the country is adapting. (BBG)  

Trump said on Saturday that a decision on Iran was coming, warning it could be resolved the “easy way or hard way.” (X)  

Saudi Aramco cut November Arab Light pricing to Asia by $3/bbl to a $5 discount to the regional benchmark, versus expectations for a $5 increase. It raised European prices by $3/bbl and left US pricing unchanged. (BBG)  

Houthis said they attacked an Aramco facility in Riyadh with missiles and drones on Saturday; witnesses reported fire and smoke near the site. (RTRS)  

Iran’s ability to target ships in Hormuz has improved, a U.S. official told WSJ, as renewed attacks threaten the recovery in Gulf exports. Commodity Context estimates flows may already have fallen 2–3mln bpd, although the preliminary figures could be revised higher. (WSJ)  

Trump said the US will not impose a diesel export ban after the G7 and partners agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks. “We’re not going to be doing the export ban,” he told reporters Friday. (BBG) 

Iran Deputy FM Gharibabadi said Sunday Iran was still reviewing the US response to its seven-day proposal; Tehran’s final position would be communicated through the appropriate channels. (Tasnim)  

Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi said there was “no military solution” to the US–Iran conflict and warned Tehran would respond more forcefully to another attack, while remaining open to fair negotiations. (Times of Israel)  

Iran’s parliament speaker Qalibaf said Hormuz would remain closed until all seven conditions under June’s Islamabad agreement are met; Washington had submitted proposals through a mediator. (Reuters)  

Iran warned neighbouring states that another attack launched from their territory would trigger a fundamentally different punitive response, urging them to reconsider facilities provided to the US and Israel. (Tasnim)  

Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad resigned citing personal reasons, state media reported, as the US blockade squeezes oil revenues. Pezeshkian appointed NIOC managing director Hamid Bovard as interim minister. (BBG)  

OPEC+ agreed to leave November production targets unchanged, maintaining its planned pause in quota increases through year-end. The seven-country group next meets on November 1. (BBG)  

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government launched a full-scale campaign to retake Houthi-held territory. Presidential Leadership Council chief Rashad Al-Alimi ordered all army branches into operations, with the Saudi-led coalition pledging full operational support. (BBG)  

US officials said Washington is providing intelligence and targeting support for Yemen’s offensive, but is avoiding direct combat for now. (Axios)  

The Pentagon withdrew all US bombers from RAF Fairford following the suspected terror plot against the base, a Defense Department official said. The NYT reported the unusually urgent withdrawal followed new information about an Iran-linked threat. (BBG) 

The oil stockpiles that cushion the world from supply shocks have become “scarily thin,” putting markets at risk of worsening unless the Strait of Hormuz reopens, according to the head of Saudi Arabia’s state producer. (BBG)

Iraq’s state tanker company arranged a VLCC carrying 2 million barrels to transport crude beyond Hormuz, taking on shipping responsibility previously left to buyers. Baghdad is also seeking funding to purchase tankers, its oil minister said. (BBG) 

At least three LNG cargoes have exited Hormuz since late last week, Bloomberg/Kpler tracking shows, extending September’s recovery. Flows remain more than 75% below pre-war levels; UKMTO reported another tanker struck inside the strait on October 4. (BBG)    

MACRO:

Bessent played down rising Treasury yields in an Axios interview, arguing the move reflects global trends rather than investors abandoning US debt. He also left open further Argentina-style financial rescues. (BBG)  

Bessent criticised AI risk warnings without proposed solutions as unhelpful “alarmism,” telling Axios that labs must accept responsibility and police themselves. He said the US cannot lose its lead to China. (BBG)  

OpenAI safety-report lead David Robinson resigned, warning that “the time for trial and error is over.” He wants frontier labs to adopt nuclear-industry-style safeguards; OpenAI maintains it is taking sufficient care. (The Atlantic)    

China’s leading AI models now trail US rivals by just 3% on benchmark scores, versus 9% in May and 15% earlier this year, Bloomberg Intelligence said. DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash gains raise questions about the durability of US AI leadership. (BBG)  

New White House AI czar Jay Clayton told WSJ his task force has 120 days to report on AI risks, opportunities and the government’s role. Officials said industry will remain primarily responsible for managing risks, while the group examines existing law and potential congressional action. (WSJ)  

Trump reiterated his pledge to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 if Republicans win both the House and Senate. Saturday’s video repeated a campaign promise, with no enacted payment programme announced. (X) 

The White House announced one-off $90 payments to more than 20 million Medicare enrollees, funded from the $2bn Medicare Improvement Fund; most eligible recipients are due direct deposits in early October. (White House)   

Hassett said Powell should leave the Fed board following the headquarters renovation report, telling Fox News it was “time for him to move on.” He also said he disagreed with September’s rate hike but respected Warsh’s reasons for supporting it. (BBG)  

Scope retained the US at AA-/stable but warned its fiscal trajectory is unsustainable and increasingly vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. The agency projects debt reaching 160% of GDP within a decade. (BBG)  

BofA’s Hartnett says it remains “risk-off until the dollar peaks,” with tighter financial conditions undermining equity breadth. Almost 60% of S&P 500 constituents are below their 200-day moving averages despite the index remaining near its highs. (BBG)  

Trump threatened further trade retaliation if South Korea fails to invest in the $54 billion Alaska LNG project. “I’ll just charge them more,” he said, after Seoul insisted participation depends on the project’s economic viability. (BBG)  

CME shelved its proposed 24/7 oil contract after industry opposition. CEO Terry Duffy cited concerns that continuous trading could introduce additional market risk; participants had warned thin weekend liquidity could distort WTI pricing. (BBG)  

Record U.S. diesel prices are pushing small trucking operators into bankruptcy, WSJ reports, with more than a dozen filing in the past month. National retail diesel recently reached $6.53/gallon, nearly $3 above a year earlier. (WSJ)  

Small businesses are still struggling to recover tariff refunds routed through parcel carriers, WSJ reports. FedEx says it must verify millions of entries, while DHL says it had returned roughly 92% of eligible customer refunds by mid-September. (WSJ)  

Japanese PM Takaichi pledged to respond to unexpected market moves and control annual debt issuance as Japan’s parliament opened. Her proposed food-tax cut remains a key priority, with its funding still unresolved. (BBG)  

BOJ Deputy Governor Uchida said AI is delivering a positive demand shock that raises inflation pressure and could affect the neutral interest rate. He also flagged competing effects from stronger equity markets and heavy tech bond issuance. (BBG) 

Japan no longer needs expansionary fiscal and monetary policies aimed at boosting demand, former Bank of Japan board member Asahi Noguchi told Reuters, projecting another interest rate hike by the central bank in December. (RTRS)

Japan's service sector expanded at a weaker pace in September as business activity and new orders grew more slowly and earthquake disruption dampened demand, a business survey showed on Monday. (RTRS)

Chinese officials requested unusual private rest arrangements and dropped a working lunch during Xi’s Washington summit, people familiar with planning told WSJ. The changes created roughly five hours of downtime; the report raises questions about his physical condition without establishing a medical diagnosis. (WSJ)   

Chinese mutual-fund closures are heading for an eight-year high as weak performance and redemptions erode assets. Bloomberg counts 256 liquidations this year, with another 46 funds warning they could close. (BBG)  

The UK is preparing tariffs on Chinese EVs to avoid exclusion from the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules, The Times reported. Officials reportedly judge the cost of exclusion greater than the risk of Chinese retaliation against JLR. (BBG)  

Prime London property values are down around 27% from their 2014 peak, or more than 49% after inflation, Bloomberg’s analysis of Savills data shows. Savills does not expect nominal price growth to return until 2028. (BBG)  

The euro fell as much as 0.8% to $1.1161, its weakest since May 2025, as European fiscal and political concerns intensified. Traders said hedge-fund selling in Asia triggered further options-related selling. (BBG)  

Hedge funds are unwinding leveraged French bond carry trades, Pimco’s Konstantin Veit told WSJ. The weekend report describes forced selling amplifying losses in positions buying French and Italian debt against Bunds or interest-rate swaps. (WSJ)  

Japanese investors hold roughly $145 billion of French bonds and remain heavily overweight relative to benchmark allocations, leaving OATs exposed to further selling. Sumitomo Mitsui DS’s global fixed-income group has already exited its French holdings. (BBG)  

Morgan Stanley IM’s Jeff Mueller said Europe is showing the first signs of sovereign-bond contagion after French weakness spread to Italy, Belgium and Greece. Persistent disorderly moves could draw policymakers’ attention, he warned. (BBG)  

Merz will meet Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos to discuss succeeding Lagarde at the ECB, Bloomberg sources said. Knot’s meeting is expected within days and de Cos’s within weeks, as negotiations over several ECB vacancies gather pace. (BBG)  

Spain’s Sánchez called a snap election for November 29 after parliament rejected his emergency housing package. The centre-right PP leads recent polling, with its leader indicating it could govern alongside Vox. (BBG) 

Rising government debt levels strengthens the case for central banks to increase their gold holdings, according to Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel. (BBG) 

A measured European Central Bank response is appropriate to control inflation as policymakers assess how a second wave of the energy shock affects the economy, according to Chief Economist Philip Lane. (BBG)

Euro zone business activity expanded at its fastest pace in nearly 3-1/2 years in September as demand remained strong despite inflation worries stemming from the Middle East war, according to an S&P survey which also showed resurgent price pressures. (RTRS)

Flávio Bolsonaro unexpectedly led Brazil’s first-round presidential vote with roughly 47% against Lula’s 45%, with counting nearly complete. The pair face an October 25 runoff, with support from eliminated candidates expected largely to favour Bolsonaro. (BBG)

Turkish September CPI slowed to 29.7% Y/Y versus 30.3% expected and 31.5% previously; monthly inflation was 1.84% versus 2.28% expected. The downside surprise strengthened expectations for an October 22 rate cut. (BBG)    

Trade deal talks between India and the United States have reached a plateau and further concessions might be difficult, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday, in the latest sign of difficulties in long-running efforts to finalise a bilateral agreement. (RTRS)

Vietnam’s PM Le Minh Hung warned that targeting 10% annual growth creates significant pressure and major challenges. He singled out increasingly difficult economic management as the government accelerates public investment. (BBG)  

GEOPOLITICAL:

Russia’s defence ministry threatened intensified attacks on Ukrainian military, industrial and related infrastructure after Zelenskyy pledged further refinery strikes. Russian forces hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge for a second time on Sunday. (BBG)  

Russian officials privately accept they are unlikely to capture Slovyansk and Kramatorsk before next year, Bloomberg sources said. Ukraine’s counteroffensive near Lyman has recovered 125 square kilometres and disrupted Moscow’s plans to seize the remaining Donetsk strongholds. (BBG)  

Zelensky said Washington proposed trilateral technical talks with Ukraine and Russia before the end of October, potentially in the UAE. Kyiv has agreed and is awaiting Moscow’s response. (X)  

Russia urged foreign diplomats to leave Kyiv on Saturday, warning that large-scale strikes on the Ukrainian capital would continue. (Russian foreign ministry)  

A multibillion-dollar deal for Lukoil’s overseas assets has become intertwined with Ukraine peace negotiations, the NYT reported; investors connected to Kushner and Witkoff are involved, with US and Russian approvals still required. (NYT)  

Merz announced approximately €1.35 billion of military and energy assistance during a surprise Kyiv visit. The package includes long-range weapons, drones and satellite technology, alongside €350 million for energy-infrastructure repairs. (BBG) 

NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defense technologies like drones and AI into traditional power. (BBG) 

The White House is monitoring a suspected plague case following an Irkutsk laboratory worker’s death; Russian authorities have not confirmed plague. (Axios)  

Netanyahu ordered a review of foreign-airline security after the FlyDubai attack. WSJ sources say Oman had barred the co-pilot from flying over radical views, but FlyDubai hired him without contacting Oman; investigators have found no links to a foreign power or major terrorist group. (WSJ)  

Taiwan’s US envoy pressed Washington to accelerate a pending $14 billion weapons package in a Bloomberg interview. A senior US administration official said Trump would decide in a fairly short time, without specifying a deadline. (BBG)  

Kim Jong Un supervised an intermediate-range missile launch using a hypersonic weapons system, KCNA reported. State media said Saturday’s missile hit a target approximately 1,000 kilometres away, with Kim pledging to keep strengthening nuclear deterrence. (BBG)  

EQUITIES:

OpenAI’s internal investigation uncovered dozens more incidents involving its agents accessing outside systems, according to the FT. Potential lawsuits and regulatory action add uncertainty to its latest fundraising efforts. (FT) 

OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public. (RTRS)

Anthropic booked over $660mn of stock-based charity-matching expenses in October–March; costs could reach billions after its IPO, diluting shareholders. (The Information)   

Qualcomm agreed to license patents underpinning Huawei’s LogicFolding chip technology through a multiyear cross-licensing agreement, Huawei said. The deal covers technologies including AI, 5G and advanced optics, validating Huawei’s push to improve chip performance despite export restrictions. (BBG)  

Apple plans tighter Mac privacy controls requiring more explicit user action before applications receive Full Disk Access. The company warned increasingly autonomous AI agents amplify the risks of granting access to messages, mail, files and browsing history. (BBG)  

Oracle and Paramount credit-default-swap costs are converging as investors increasingly treat their Larry Ellison exposure as linked. Money managers warned Oracle’s AI spending could weaken the family’s financial backstop just when Paramount needs support. (BBG)  

Elon Musk confirmed discussions with TSMC over his Texas chipmaking project, saying: “Just discussions, but something may come of it.” A signed Terafab agreement has not been confirmed. (Musk on X)  

OpenAI CEO Altman pushed back on speculation about OpenAI’s Cerebras relationship: “Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed.” (Altman on X)  

Irrational Analysis argues the reported 25% performance/power delta between revisions of OpenAI’s Broadcom-built Jalapeño chip signals a serious design or validation problem. This is the author’s assessment, challenging SemiAnalysis’s more positive interpretation. (Irrational Analysis)  

The FAA determined a Boeing 737 MAX software glitch does not constitute a flight-safety issue, easing a potential obstacle to MAX 10 certification. Boeing will issue guidance on recognising and responding to the problem while working on a software update. (WSJ)

More than 20 NHS trusts have stopped using Palantir’s waiting-list tools, according to FT analysis, highlighting deployment and performance issues in its healthcare rollout. (FT)  

Foxconn reported on Monday a 47% jump in third-quarter revenue year-on-year that beat market estimates, fuelled by strong AI-related demand. (RTRS)

Analysts expect TSMC’s 2027 price increases to reach 5–10% for advanced processes and 10–15% for advanced packaging. Pricing and next year’s capex are key focuses for its 15 October earnings call. (Commercial Times)  

Samsung is reportedly seeking 2027 HBM4 prices more than three times its current HBM3E prices, industry sources said. The report describes asking prices as next-generation memory ramps. (DigiTimes) 

AI data centres’ aggressive buying of LPDDR5X is expected to sustain memory price pressure on PCs and smartphones through H1 2027, according to industry sources cited by DigiTimes. (DigiTimes)   

SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son warned that superintelligence in the wrong hands could become “super dangerous,” urging international cooperation at a Kyoto event. The comments mark a rare public note of caution from one of AI’s biggest financial backers. (BBG)  

Schneider agreed to acquire PTC for $22.6 billion in cash, paying $205/share—a premium exceeding 40% to Friday’s close. Its largest-ever acquisition is expected to complete by Q3 2027; Schneider shares fell as much as 7.6%. (BBG)  

Air Liquide on Monday launched a €4 billion ($4.5 billion) share buyback plan and said it aimed to raise its operating margin by 400 to 600 basis points by 2030 as part of a new mid-term strategy.  (RTRS)

Monte Paschi’s largest shareholder Delfin agreed to tender its entire 17.6% holding into Intesa’s improved €34.6 billion bid. Intesa has said it will abandon the offer if Paschi shareholders approve its CEO’s rival acquisition plans on October 29. (BBG)

text:
An intelligence-led operation by a combined team of troops of the  Nigerian Army, Department of Department of State Services (DSS)  personnel, and Western Nigeria Security Network aka Amotekun officers, at the weekend in Owo forest, Ondo State, eliminated a senior leader of the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), Abdussamad Ohida.

Security sources said Ohida aka Anwar, who was on the verge of planning massive terrorist attacks in some southern states, was killed alongside many members of the terrorist organization by the security forces who led a surprise attack on their forest hideout.

According to the sources, the eliminated ISWAP leader previously served as deputy to ISWAP Central Nigeria leader Abu Ikrimah, also known as Abu Uwais. Ikrimah was arrested by the DSS in 2023. 

Following Ikrimah's arrest, continued the sources, Ohida assumed leadership of ISWAP activities across parts of North central and southern parts of the country, where he subsequently played a key role in the planning, coordination and execution of terrorist operations.

Through the interrogation of Abu Uwais, continued the sources, the DSS was able to gather credible intelligence on plans by Ohida to 
attack innocent persons during the forthcoming Yuletide. 
"The plan was to attack civilians during the festive period and ultimately disrupt the 2027 general elections. This Intelligence was corroborated by intelligence partners from the United Kingdom, who supported the elimination operation," offered one of the sources.

He said Ohida planned and executed the 31st December 2025, invasion of Ipele Divisional Police Station, Owo, Ondo State, carting away right AK-47 rifles before bringing down the station with an explosive. He mentioned the 28 July 2022 Suleja–Zuba Road, Niger State military checkpoint attack in which several soldiers, officers and civilians were killed.

He also blamed on Ohida, the July 11, 2022, attack on Kuje Correctional Centre, Abuja; the 23rd April, 2022 attack on Ogaminana Police Station, Adavi LGA, Kogi State, which resulted in the death of five police officers, and the February 7, 2022, attack on Okene Area Command police station.

"The terrorist planned and executed the 24th December, 2020 attack on a Naval checkpoint in Okene, Kogi State, which resulted in the death of two naval officers, not to mention the several attacks he launched across parts of the country," he added.
"We may not immediately realize it, but the elimination of Abdussamad Ohida represents a significant disruption to ISWAP’s leadership structure, operational network and expansion efforts in central and southern Nigeria.

"Ohida's elimination, coming a few months after after the killing of ISIS leader Abu Bilal al-Minuki, is a very big blow to ISWAP’s efforts to expand its operational presence in Nigeria, and underscores the growing efficiency of our security services," he declared.

LADY OF COURAGE: Hope Anne Anguyo has become the first woman to drive the Archbishop of the @ChurchofUganda_, The Most Rev Dr Stephen Samuel Kaziimba Mugalu, in Uganda.

Here is how it happened, unexpectedly!

Hope is a farmer and the proprietor of Le Tsuba Hotel in Arua City, where the Archbishop and his team have been residing during his farewell visit to Madi West Nile Diocese.

Yesterday morning, Archbishop Kaziimba was scheduled to commission Christ Church Ediofe at 9:00am, commission the Diocesan Golden Jubilee Office Block, and later attend the farewell service at Emmanuel Cathedral, Mvara.

Then, just a few minutes before departure, the Archbishop’s car got a flat tyre! 

The Bishop of Madi West Nile Diocese, Rt Rev Charles Collins Andaku, had already arrived to pick him up. Bishop Andaku is a man of very few words, but one thing about him: he keeps time to the dot! 

As we were still figuring out how to handle the situation, Hope quickly offered a solution, she offered to drive the Archbishop.
And off we went!

What followed was a fascinating conversation as she drove, playing soft gospel music. I won’t reveal the type of Car she drives, but all I can say it was an extremely clean car with a beautiful scent and air conditioning.

Along the way, Hope shared some brilliant ideas about how the Church can make better use of its vast land by investing in commercial agriculture. She pointed out that hundreds of trucks bring tomatoes, rice and other foodstuffs into Arua City, with some proceeding across the border into the Democratic Republic of Congo. Why shouldn't the Church tap into this huge market?

She also spoke passionately about preparing clergy for retirement, noting that many clergy fear retirement because they are not adequately prepared financially. She believes the Church can explore sustainable investments that enable clergy to retire with greater security and dignity.

@HCT_Direcorate will further this discussion and bring it to an implementation conclusion.

And by the way, when you are in Arua City, check out Le Tsuba Hotel. Hope says Le Tsuba means “the sharp edge of the sword” which reaffirms their commitment to sharp, quality service.

I’m very full. Thank you.

He practiced carefully.

The next day, Mama smiled.

“Ah, kabalo na!”

Oh, he knows already!

Then she packed food for later.

Protest continues outside Georgian prison over inmate’s sexual assault allegations

A protest is continuing outside a prison in Rustavi, Georgia, as the family of an inmate who says he was sexually assaulted by prison guards demands that he be transferred to another facility.

The family of 36-year-old Giorgi Davitadze says the guards he has accused of sexual assault are still working at Rustavi’s No. 6 penitentiary, where he remains imprisoned. They say he is being subjected to pressure and psychological intimidation and are calling for his transfer.

The latest dispute began after the penitentiary service said Davitadze swallowed an unidentified small object on the evening of 4 October. According to the service, he did so deliberately in front of a prison employee. He was offered transfer to a medical clinic but refused, and prison medical staff are monitoring him around the clock, officials said.

Davitadze has alleged that on 21 December 2025, around 10 prison guards sexually assaulted him in a de-escalation room at the same facility. He says the incident was captured by security cameras and that he later attempted suicide.

The Special Penitentiary Service has categorically denied the allegation, saying there was no sexual or other physical violence against him. It has released video footage of the incident, but the recording has no sound.

Davitadze’s family and supporters are demanding that the full footage, including audio, be made public and that the case be independently investigated. They also want the head of the prison to resign.

Georgia’s Public Defender, Levan Ioseliani, said his office had examined the available footage but had not seen evidence of violence. He has nevertheless called attention to the allegations and the need to establish what happened. More than 10 civil society organisations have also called for an effective and comprehensive investigation, saying the footage released by the penitentiary service cannot substitute for an independent investigation.

Remembering 
Barbara Marie Nickerauer  known professionally as Barbara Nichols, was an American actress who often played brassy or comic roles in films in the 1950s and 1960s.

Early in her career, Nichols was a showgirl when a club owner offered her a much higher salary to perform striptease. She declined the offer, keeping her focus on becoming an actress.

She began modeling for cheesecake magazines in the late 1940s and eventually was considered a minor rival to Marilyn Monroe. On Broadway, she appeared in the 1952 revival of Pal Joey (she also appeared in the 1957 film version) and in Let It Ride (1961).

In the mid-1950s, she moved to Hollywood and began appearing in showy supporting roles in A-films, such as Miracle in the Rain (1956), The King and Four Queens (1956), The Naked and the Dead (1958), The Pajama Game (1957), Sweet Smell of Success (1957), 

That Kind of Woman (1958), and Where the Boys Are (1960), with high-profile actors, including Clark Gable, Susan Hayward, Sophia Loren, and Doris Day. One of her few starring roles was in the 1965 science-fiction film The Human Duplicators. Her final film was Won Ton Ton, the Dog Who Saved Hollywood in 1976.

Susan Kuhnhausen fought for her life when a hitman tried to kill her in a murder-for-hire plot orchestrated by her husband... 

On September 6, 2006, Susan Kuhnhausen came home from work and found a stranger waiting inside her bedroom with a claw hammer.

He had been waiting for hours.

Susan was 51, an emergency room nurse in Portland, Oregon. The man lunged at her and struck her in the head. She fought back, wrestled away the hammer, lost it again, and found herself locked in a brutal struggle with a man who seemed determined to kill her.

Susan began thinking like someone who expected to die.

She bit him repeatedly, hoping that if he killed her, investigators would find her teeth marks on his body. While they fought, she tried reaching into his pockets for identification she could throw somewhere police might discover it.

But Susan didn’t die.

After roughly 14 minutes, she managed to climb on top of him and lock her arm around his neck.

Then she offered him a way out.

“Tell me who sent you here and I will call you a fu*king ambulance!”

The man refused to answer.

Susan tightened her hold until he stopped moving, grabbed the hammer and ran to a neighbor’s house. The attacker, 59-year-old Edward Haffey, was dead.

At first, it looked like a horrifying home invasion.

Then investigators started finding things.

There was no forced entry. Haffey had worked for Susan’s estranged husband, Michael Kuhnhausen. A backpack contained Michael’s new phone number and a day planner with an entry reading, “Call Mike.”

The truth was worse than Susan had imagined.

Her husband had arranged to have her killed and the scene made to look like a burglary. Prosecutors said Haffey had been offered $50,000.

Michael eventually pleaded guilty and was sentenced to ten years in prison.

Susan later changed her surname to Walters and devoted part of her life to helping other crime victims.

The man sent into her home believed he was there to kill a middle-aged nurse.

Instead, the nurse walked out.

He didn’t.

How should a Christian view relics?
Answer
A splinter from Jesus’ cross has been found in Turkey. Jesus’ baby blanket has surfaced in Germany. The index finger of John the Baptist is now on display in a reliquary in a Missouri museum. Relics—carefully preserved religious artifacts meant to be venerated—have long played a role in many religions, including Christianity. By the Middle Ages, there were hundreds of supposed burial places for the twelve apostles. It has been said that one could build a large boat from all the pieces of wood purported to be from Jesus’ cross. The most famous Christian relic, the Shroud of Turin, attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors each year. Should Christians be interested in relics?

Undeniably, it would be extremely interesting if an actual piece of Jesus’ cross or a thorn from the crown of thorns could be discovered and verified. The problem is that there is absolutely no way to know if a piece of Judean wood dates to the 1st century A.D. Someone could claim it came from Jesus’ cross, but how could that claim be substantiated? The wood could just as easily have come from a Judean fence post. In the early centuries of the Roman Catholic Church, relics became a massive profiteering scam. Seemingly every church throughout Europe had some sort of relic to attract visitors. If a church in a nearby town “discovered” a more important relic, a game of one-upmanship ensued, with the relics being “discovered” becoming more and more impressive. All that to say, it is highly unlikely that any of the Christian relics discovered in the past 2,000 years have any true connection to Jesus or the apostles.

One of the dangers inherent in the veneration of relics is the temptation to commit idolatry. This is exactly what happened in ancient Israel. God had told Moses to make a bronze serpent in order to save the Hebrews from a plague of poisonous snakes (Numbers 21:8–9). That bronze serpent was kept by the Israelites as a reminder of God’s goodness and salvation; however, by the time of King Hezekiah, the “relic” had become an object of worship. Hezekiah’s reforms included breaking “into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had been burning incense to it. (It was called Nehushtan)” (2 Kings 18:4). Physical aids to faith, if not commanded by God, are unnecessary and inevitably lead to superstition and idolatry.

The pope's apology in Canada was historic, but for some Indigenous people, not enough
Updated July 25, 2022 7:10 PM ET 
By 
Scott Neuman
Years after a Canadian-government-funded commission issued findings detailing a history of physical and sexual abuse of Indigenous children in the country's Catholic-run residential schools, Pope Francis on Monday issued an apology on Canadian soil.

"I am sorry," the pope said, speaking in Maskwacis, Alberta, at the lands of four Cree nations.

"I humbly beg forgiveness for the evil committed by so many Christians against the Indigenous peoples," Francis said near the site of the former Ermineskin Indian Residential School, where ground-penetrating radar has been used to try to locate unmarked graves of students who died while attending the school.

The residential schools forcibly separated Indigenous children from their parents as part of an effort to convert them to Christianity and assimilate them into the wider Canadian culture. In total, 150,000 children from Canada's First Nations tribes were placed in 139 schools run under government contract — most by the Catholic Church — over a 150-year period.

A 2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission report prompted by the harrowing tales of survivors concluded that "[children] were abused, physically and sexually, and they died in the schools in numbers that would not have been tolerated in any school system anywhere in the country."

The schools were designed "not to educate" the Indigenous children, "but primarily to break their link to their culture and identity," the report said. It concluded that the establishment and operation of the schools "can best be described as 'cultural genocide.'"

Morning Market Report 🌞 Monday, October 5, 2026

Opening Perspective: Consumer Sentiment and Midterm Precedent

Historically, no governing political party—Republican or Democrat—has successfully held control of the U.S. House of Representatives during a midterm cycle when the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index sat deeply depressed below the 50 mark. The only prior historical period in which sentiment traded near current depressed levels was during the mid-1970s stagflation era and the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis; in both instances, the party controlling the White House suffered major congressional seat losses. With consumer sentiment lingering around 47.8 to 48 heading into this week's fresh economic print, history suggests substantial political headwinds for the incumbent party in November.  Indeed, I have hypothecated the Republican Party is delusional if they think they stand a chance to win midterms given the high inflation.  Nobody listens.  

Macro Analysis: Persistent Inflationary Factors and Economic PressureThe current weakness in consumer sentiment reflects persistent cost-of-living pressures, lingering high energy prices, and stagnant real wage growth. These headwinds continue to weigh heavily on household balance sheets, constraining discretionary consumer spending and subduing broader economic momentum as we enter the fourth quarter. Moreover, borrowing costs remain elevated, with key fixed interest rates holding near multi-year highs and further dampening real estate transactions and big-ticket retail volume.

Labor Market and Fiscal DynamicsAdding to the cautious sentiment, recent employment metrics reveal a noticeable slowdown in gross hiring across key corporate sectors. While widespread layoffs remain relatively isolated, labor market friction is becoming evident as open position counts decline and national unemployment ticks upward. Market participants are closely evaluating whether corporate profit margins can withstand higher input costs without triggering additional labor market contraction or broader earnings revisions.

The Week Ahead: Market Outlook and Data DriversAs trading opens for the week, market indexes remain sensitive to upcoming macroeconomic updates, including the latest consumer sentiment readings and inflation prints. Investors should expect elevated volatility across equities and fixed income as traders digest potential shifts in Federal Reserve policy expectations alongside ongoing geopolitical developments. Market dynamics will likely center on whether corporate guidance can offer support against an increasingly guarded macro environment.

The rhetoric on Capitol Hill is bound to reach a fever pitch, but what’s happening across the pond serves as a stark, real-time case study in economic consequences. While Washington gets bogged down in endless hyper-partisan theater, the UK is offering a textbook lesson in capital flight—showing precisely what happens when populist tax policies collide with global mobility.

When you raise tax burdens on high earners and wealth creators beyond a critical threshold, capital doesn't stand still and take it; it packs its bags. Francine Lacqua’s surprise on Bloomberg this AM reflects a broader consensus gap: policymakers often assume a captive audience, yet high-net-worth individuals, entrepreneurs, and investment capital are inherently mobile. London’s aggressive tax shifts are driving a silent exit to low-tax jurisdictions like Dubai, Switzerland, Greece, and Singapore, taking tax revenues, job creation, and economic dynamism right along with them.

If American Democratic lawmakers are too distracted by their own soundbites and table-pounding to pay attention to the European model, they risk repeating the exact same policy errors. Heading into the next two years, the real test won't be which party scores more political points on television, but whether Washington can avoid making the kind of heavy-handed regulatory and fiscal missteps that end up driving American capital, talent, and innovation elsewhere.

All this work to get here, and the Republicans just give it away.  This unforced error may not be recoverable.  Damage will be done.

“I’m thinking about transferring.”

At Nagoya there was an absolute presence in Hideomi Fukatsu (36), who served as the starting setter for the Japan men’s national team in the 2026 season. The backup setters were Kamibayashi plus Shinonosuke Hayasaka (26), now with the Hokkaido Yellow Stars, and playing time was limited.

On top of that, Ryogo Maeda (23)—once called the number-one setter in college—was joining from Waseda University.

“Even in the Emperor’s Cup I couldn’t contribute as a force, and honestly there were times I wondered, ‘Why aren’t they using me?’ I also started to feel that maybe I was no longer being considered part of the team’s strength. It was hard to win the coach’s trust, and from around the Emperor’s Cup I began seriously thinking about a transfer.”

At 27 he stood at a crossroads. Some players might see that age as the point when a career comes to an end.

But retiring was not an option for Kamibayashi.

There was a reason.

After graduating from Meiji University, he once took a job in his home prefecture of Yamagata and continued playing volleyball with a local club team.

In the autumn of 2023, his third year as a working adult, he finished seventh at the National Sports Festival (now the National Sports Games) as a member of the Yamagata prefectural select team. Through various connections, in December 2023 he took part in the “Japan men’s national team promising young players camp,” which mainly gathered university players. That led to an offer from Nagoya. After some hesitation he quit his company and decided to join in 2024.

“When I left the company, I decided I wanted to keep playing volleyball until my body truly couldn’t move anymore, and I turned pro. If I quit now it would feel unfinished, and I wouldn’t be able to end it in a way I could accept.”

“I love Wolfdogs, but… I want to play.”

Yet that thirst rising from the bottom of his heart was matched by an equally strong love for the team.

“Wolfdogs is a wonderful environment where you can focus only on volleyball, the players all get along, and the staff and office people were all warm. In truth, part of me wanted to stay with this team until the end.”

Italian coach Valerio Baldovin aims for volleyball at the world’s cutting edge, and after Kamibayashi joined he was taught setting again from scratch.

The coach insists on “actions that lead to winning,” and sought intention in every action—not only in practice, but even in how players eat and rest in their private lives. Kamibayashi’s awareness of how he approached volleyball day to day changed greatly, and that showed in his actions.

Playing time was scarce, but in roughly two years at Nagoya he felt he had grown a great deal—not only in his play and his thinking, but as a person.

Above all, the gratitude and sense of obligation for being brought into the top league after he had been a working adult were huge. He could not decide right away. While talking with various people, he also consulted Tomohiro Ogawa (30), now with Lublin—two years his senior at Meiji and, for a time, a teammate at Nagoya.

“I like the team Wolfdogs, and I got in thanks to Tomo-san (Ogawa) and various other people. So part of me wants to do it with this team.” Ogawa replied:

“No, you don’t really need to think about that. It’s better to go somewhere you can play, and better to keep challenging yourself. You want to play in matches, right?”
