text:
An Iranian Threat, 3 Vans and a Phone Call: Behind the Mystery at a U.K. Air Base

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 12:48 min
Published 03OCT2026 & Updated 04OCT2026
By Michael D. Shear, Eric Schmitt, Megan Specia, and Adam Goldman
https://t.co/ChdUDBfCD5
Michael D. Shear and Adam Goldman reported from London, Megan Specia from Fairford, England, and Eric Schmitt from Washington.

A mysterious call last Sunday near a military base used by the U.S. set in motion a huge counterterrorism response and days of uncertainty in Britain.

The three white vans navigated through a picturesque stretch of rural England in the middle of the night, winding toward a British air base that America is using to wage war on Iran.

It was 12:45 a.m. on Sunday when one of the men inside the vans 

— for reasons still not clear — 

dialed emergency services, giving authorities their first sign that a terrorism plot they had received intelligence on almost two weeks earlier might be in motion.

The police scrambled an urgent, armed response, speeding to the scene and arresting the man and four associates. 

A grainy photo later leaked to the media showed the five men sitting shirtless on the side of a road, their hands bound behind their backs.

Five arrested as counter-terror police investigate major incident near RAF Fairford
https://t.co/T0efWnPSQc
29SEP2026 Olivia Ireland & Leigh Boobyer, West of England

Why the man called the police remains the subject of debate among investigators trying to unravel what happened that night, security officials from several countries told The New York Times. They asked for anonymity because the inquiry remains open.

It is one of many puzzles that the authorities have yet to piece together.

The call did set off a cascade of events, including the arrest of the men on suspicion of terrorism, the frantic evacuation of 85 homes, a bomb disposal robot searching the vans for explosives, and a national security meeting convened by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. 

He said later that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part.”

But a part in what, exactly? Mr. Burnham and other British authorities have offered few answers. The vans contained no explosives when the police searched them. 

And within a day, all five men were released on bail, the kind of treatment typically given to common criminals, rather than terrorism suspects. 

The authorities could also have been hamstrung by the need to keep evidence classified and thus unable to be cited in criminal court.

The police have cast a wide net in trying to find those responsible for hiring the men, whom one official described as “unwitting chumps.” 

U.S. and British officials believe the operation is connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps or a separate military headquarters in Tehran. Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, has rejected the accusations.

This account is drawn from interviews with investigators, local officials and residents as well as security officials in Britain, Germany, Israel and the United States who had knowledge of warnings about a plot to target U.S. bases in Britain and Europe. 

Some officials declined to reveal details of the case. 

Others conceded that the full story remains hazy, even to them. 

Most spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing the sensitive nature of the investigation.

For Britain, the events of the last six days have been a vivid — if at times mystifying — reminder that the American- and Israeli-led war against Iran that began eight months ago has the potential to do more than raise the price of oil.

In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards issued a statement warning that allowing the United States to use the base “makes London responsible” for their actions. 

“Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory,” the statement said, “is a legitimate target for our forces.”

Officials found no concrete signs the men in the vans were in the final stages of an attack.

Then, over the weekend, commanders received new information, which one U.S. official said was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced last month but with specific details and greater urgency. 

The U.S. rapidly withdrew all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from the air base, two U.S. officials said on Sunday, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
05OCT2026
By Eric Schmitt 
https://t.co/nUA7uo65Cn
The withdrawal came with unusual speed, following what U.S. officials said were threats of an Iran-based plot against the installation.
A military airplane taking flight in an airfield with a lightly cloudy sky in the background.

Vague warnings
In mid-September, U.S. military commanders received a chilling warning from American and other Western intelligence agencies, according to U.S. officials briefed on the information. 

R.A.F. Fairford, the base in southern England primarily used by the United States Air Force to deploy some of its largest bombers, was the target of a potential Iran-backed attack.

The map locates the R.A.F. Fairford air base, outside of the city of Fairford, in southern England, northwest of London.

The murky outlines of a plot had been pieced together through a combination of intercepted communications, informants and other intelligence. 

Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said his intelligence officials also warned their British counterparts of a probable Iranian-sponsored attack, though they did not provide a specific target. 

Follow-up attacks were likely to include drones, the confidential assessments warned.

The warnings were general. Analysts could not pin down a date or concrete details about the plotters, other than concluding they were guided and supported by Tehran. Base commanders in Britain raised security levels, already elevated since the start of the war with Iran.

Residents of the nearby town of Fairford, and the villages of Kempsford and Whelford, began noticing changes. There were “rumbles that things were being moved around the base in terms of protection and levels of warnings,” said Dom Morris, a local councilor.

On Sept. 16, 11 days before the episode at the base, a resident posted in a private neighborhood Facebook group that he had seen something unusual: a man in a balaclava running through the village around 9 p.m. At least three other villagers said they had seen a masked man wearing black. It was unclear if they were speaking about the same person, or who it was.

Across Europe, concern among officials was surging. 

According to a senior U.S. official, Israel warned Germany that American bases there were at heightened risk, noting Spangdahlem and Ramstein in particular.

On Sept. 23, four days before the events at R.A.F. Fairford, an Iranian-backed media site posted comments from Yahya Rahim Safavi, former chief commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. 

According to SITE Intelligence Group, which tracks the online activity of jihadist organizations, Mr. Safavi condemned Europe as a “logistics hub” for America’s war on Iran, naming air bases that U.S. forces have used to conduct the war, including Ramstein in Germany, Aviano in Italy and Fairford.

But without concrete intelligence about a specific target or timing, there was little the authorities could do — except tighten security and wait.

A plot emerges
That changed, dramatically, last Sunday.

A local farmer returning home from a party found her driveway blocked by the three white vans.

“I looked at it and thought, ‘That is not real,’” the farmer, who declined to be identified, later told BBC News. 

She told reporters she saw eight to 10 people in masks running.

At 1:36 a.m., she said, she called 999, the British version of 911, and later said she believed her call “foiled whatever plans they had.”

The police timeline suggests, however, that she made her call about 50 minutes after the man in the van. It isn’t clear whether the people she saw were the suspects, or security operatives responding to the initial alert.

“This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation,” Vicki Evans, the deputy assistant commissioner for Britain’s counter terrorism police, said later on Sunday, adding, “Our activity is in the interest of national security.”

By Monday, however, the case took a surprising turn.

The men were released on bail, a rare outcome for terrorism suspects. The police said later they had discovered some gasoline, but no explosives, in the vans. Laurence Taylor, Ms. Evans’s supervisor, told reporters the men were “subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation.”

Behind closed doors, officials were trying to determine the suspects’ role, and whether Iran was using them to undermine Britain’s willingness to let the United States use its bases. It is not yet clear how much investigators have learned from the men about their plans.

Were they a diversion from another attack that was in the works? Had they been intercepted before they could link up with other confederates? Or was the episode an elaborate hoax designed to sow fear and create propaganda?

Some intelligence officials believed the initial call by one of the five men was part of a plan to distract the police while a broader plot unfolded. Others thought it was more likely that the five men were low-level criminals, one of whom called when they realized they had been hired to do something serious.

Mr. Taylor shared little about the investigation in his statement on Monday. But he hinted at the complexity of the case.

“Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity,” he said, “often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain.”

Assessing future risks
The head of MI5, Britain’s domestic security agency, has warned for years about Iran-backed plots, which have often involved targeting opponents using local criminals.

“Iranian state actors make extensive use of criminals as proxies — from international drug traffickers to low-level crooks,” Ken McCallum, the group’s director general, said in 2024. Iranian journalists and dissidents in Britain have received death threats and been physically attacked.

When he was prime minister of Britain, Keir Starmer initially refused to let the Trump administration use R.A.F. Fairford for strikes on Iran, saying he would not join “regime change from the skies.” 

But he later gave permission for what he called “defensive” operations, and American B-52 and B-1 planes loaded with bombs began flying to Iran from Fairford. Mr. Burnham has continued the policy.

After Mr. Starmer announced the change on March 1, Iranian proxies appeared ready to act against a wider range of targets in Britain. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer group in London were set on fire. Molotov cocktails were thrown at several synagogues in the middle of the night.

The goal appeared to be to stoke fear in the Jewish community, while signaling that Britain’s changed posture had consequences. 

The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, or Hayi, which, U.S. prosecutors said, is a front for Kataib Hezbollah, a U.S.-designated terrorist group and one of the most powerful Iranian proxies in Iraq. 

A commander from the group was charged in the United States in May with leading the attacks and other incidents in Europe as part of a retaliation campaign by Tehran.

In April, Hayi posted a video claiming that the Israeli Embassy in London would be attacked by drones carrying dangerous substances. Suspicious items, including two jars of a powdered substance, were found in the nearby Kensington Gardens. A huge police response was triggered, involving chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear teams. But the police later concluded that there had been no attack on the embassy and the powdered substance was not hazardous.

An actual assault on an American air base in Britain would be a drastic escalation, officials said.

By the end of the week, the evacuated families had returned to their homes and a 1,300-foot cordon around where the vans had been was taken down. But concrete barriers were installed around the entrance of R.A.F. Fairford. As the investigation continued, the police arrested a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian citizen in London, on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. He, too, was released on bail.

Julian E. Barnes contributed reporting from Washington.

Michael D. Shear is the chief U.K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U.S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Megan Specia reports on Britain, Ireland and the Ukraine war for The Times. She is based in London.

Adam Goldman is a London-based reporter for The Times who writes about global security.

A version of this article appears in print on Oct. 4, 2026, Section A, Page 12 of the New York edition with the headline: A Threat, 3 Vans and a Shadow War in a Corner of England.

Automated turrets offer another layer of defense. Machine vision can help detect and track fast-moving targets, while automation shortens the engagement cycle.

text:
$ONEN: Headquartered in West Palm Beach, Florida, the company positions itself as an independent power developer. Its strategy involves deploying natural gas units and energy storage systems for rapid implementation, supplemented by advanced Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) in the long term, to provide high-density baseload power to data centers, hydrogen facilities, industrial sites, and the grid, while securing long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). The industry backdrop is characterized by surging electricity demand from AI data centers and a race across the Southeastern U.S. (particularly Louisiana) to secure transmission capacity, industrial parks, and computing infrastructure sites. While the nuclear power narrative is gaining momentum, natural gas combined with energy storage remains the only solution capable of grid interconnection within two to three years; SMRs require site selection, environmental impact assessments, and U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing—a process spanning a decade. ONEN sits at the very beginning of this value chain: it holds site control intentions but currently lacks permits, disclosed off-takers, and operating revenue.
On September 23, 2026, the company completed its merger with Hennessy Capital Investment Corp. VII and began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ONEN around September 24. It closed at approximately $1.87 on October 2, with a market capitalization of roughly $200–$230 million; the stock has fallen about 82% over the past 52 weeks, with insiders holding approximately 74% of shares and institutions holding about 4%. In pre-market trading on October 5, the price briefly touched approximately $1.95.

Product and Qualification Highlights
The company’s offering is not currently operational power plants, but rather a portfolio of three projects in Louisiana totaling approximately 5 GW under development. This includes "Amberjack," a standalone, scalable multi-unit SMR complex targeting up to approximately 1 GW of advanced nuclear capacity. Site control has been secured, and the project has entered the technical and environmental assessment phase, with preparations underway for pre-application discussions with the NRC. The company has clarified that current activities do not equate to NRC site approval, reactor licensing, environmental permits, or a finalized engineering plan; specific reactor designs, investment budgets, commercial operation dates, and power customers have not yet been determined. Cayman: ~2.88 GW of natural gas-fired generation paired with ~700 MW / 2.88 GWh of energy storage, with the potential to co-locate a data center campus. A binding Letter of Intent (LOI) for site control was signed with a local landowner group in late August 2026; the site is located near RiverPlex MegaPark, northeast of the area where SpaceX is currently expanding its infrastructure. The current plan does not include nuclear power.
Barracuda: ~1.2 GW of modular natural gas generation, ~300 MW / 1.2 GWh of four-hour energy storage, and up to ~1 GW of critical IT data center capacity; deployment can be phased based on customer demand and grid interconnection conditions.

Core Investment Thesis: The narrative aligns with the pressing issue of power shortages: AI data centers require 24/7 power; gas-fired generation plus storage offers a near-term solution, while SMRs represent a long-term option.
The Louisiana portfolio combines ~4 GW of gas-fired generation and up to 1 GW of nuclear capacity on a single platform; securing a major customer for either project could drive significant valuation upside.
The stock price has retreated significantly from its highs during the initial listing hype; the market cap of ~$200 million reflects the value of "5 GW under development" options rather than operational assets.
High insider ownership aligns interests with project advancement; however, the low public float and limited institutional holdings make the price susceptible to one-sided volatility driven by news flow.

Short-term target price: $1.60–$2.30
